findings.measured: Loudness is -10.7 LUFS; typical for Trap / hip-hop is -9 to -6 LUFS.

steps.text: Raise Limiter's Gain in 1 dB steps until you reach the target; keep Ceiling at −1.0 dB.

other_options.text: Before bouncing, play the whole song through a loudness meter and check integrated LUFS and true peak.

notes.headline: This master is technically clean at 10/10 — the only open question is loudness, sitting at -10.7 LUFS where trap and hip-hop usually land between -9 and -6 LUFS.
notes.summary: Nothing here is broken: true peak is -2.16 dBTP, left/right balance is within -0.04 dB, and the stereo picture holds together in mono with only 0.51 dB of loss. The one thing to weigh is level — at -10.72 LUFS integrated you're a couple of dB under where trap and hip-hop masters typically sit, so this may feel soft next to other tracks in a playlist. That's a judgement call, not an error, and you have 8.6 dB of peak-to-loudness and 2.16 dB of true-peak room to work with if you decide to push.

priorities.title: Decide on final loudness
priorities.why: At -10.7 LUFS the track will read quieter than most trap and hip-hop releases played back-to-back with it. You have the headroom to close the gap if that's the goal, but only do it if the low end and transients hold up.

listen_for: After each 1 dB step on the Limiter, check whether the 808s and kick stay punchy or start to flatten and pump — that's your stopping point, not the meter.
Compare the louder version against the current bounce at matched level on headphones; if the louder one doesn't sound better matched, keep the quieter one.
Play the whole 40 seconds through a loudness meter before the final bounce and confirm integrated LUFS and true peak with the Ceiling still at -1.0 dB.
strengths: True peak at -2.16 dBTP leaves safe room for lossy encoding.
Left/right balance is essentially centred at -0.04 dB.
Mono compatibility is solid — only 0.51 dB of level loss in mono, with low-end correlation at 0.78.
